questiontext.text:
Without calculating, decide whether each estimate is an overestimate, an underestimate or the exact area.

First decide whether each curve bends upwards, bends downwards or is a straight line on its interval.

  1. The {@rr[1]@} rule with \(4\) strips for \(y = {@fr[1]@}\) from \(x = {@lr[1]@}\) to \(x = {@hr[1]@}\) gives [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]
  2. The {@rr[2]@} rule with \(4\) strips for \(y = {@fr[2]@}\) from \(x = {@lr[2]@}\) to \(x = {@hr[2]@}\) gives [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]
  3. The {@rr[3]@} rule with \(4\) strips for \(y = {@fr[3]@}\) from \(x = {@lr[3]@}\) to \(x = {@hr[3]@}\) gives [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]]
  4. The {@rr[4]@} rule with \(4\) strips for \(y = {@fr[4]@}\) from \(x = {@lr[4]@}\) to \(x = {@hr[4]@}\) gives [[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]]
  5. The {@rr[5]@} rule with \(4\) strips for \(y = {@fr[5]@}\) from \(x = {@lr[5]@}\) to \(x = {@hr[5]@}\) gives [[input:ans5]] [[validation:ans5]]
[[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
For a curve that bends upwards the chords lie above the curve, so the trapezoidal rule overestimates; the mid-ordinate rule errs the other way and underestimates. For a curve that bends downwards both are reversed. For a straight line both rules give the exact area. The second derivative tells the bend: positive on the interval means it bends upwards.

  1. \(y = {@fr[1]@}\), \({@lr[1]@} \le x \le {@hr[1]@}\): \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = {@diff(fr[1],x,2)@}\), [[if test="is(pm[1]<=2)"]]never negative on this interval, so the curve bends upwards[[elif test="is(pm[1]<=4)"]]never positive on this interval, so the curve bends downwards[[else]]so the graph is a straight line[[/if]]. The {@rr[1]@} rule gives [[if test="is(pm[1]=1 or pm[1]=4)"]]an overestimate[[elif test="is(pm[1]=5)"]]the exact area[[else]]an underestimate[[/if]].

  2. \(y = {@fr[2]@}\), \({@lr[2]@} \le x \le {@hr[2]@}\): \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = {@diff(fr[2],x,2)@}\), [[if test="is(pm[2]<=2)"]]never negative on this interval, so the curve bends upwards[[elif test="is(pm[2]<=4)"]]never positive on this interval, so the curve bends downwards[[else]]so the graph is a straight line[[/if]]. The {@rr[2]@} rule gives [[if test="is(pm[2]=1 or pm[2]=4)"]]an overestimate[[elif test="is(pm[2]=5)"]]the exact area[[else]]an underestimate[[/if]].

  3. \(y = {@fr[3]@}\), \({@lr[3]@} \le x \le {@hr[3]@}\): \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = {@diff(fr[3],x,2)@}\), [[if test="is(pm[3]<=2)"]]never negative on this interval, so the curve bends upwards[[elif test="is(pm[3]<=4)"]]never positive on this interval, so the curve bends downwards[[else]]so the graph is a straight line[[/if]]. The {@rr[3]@} rule gives [[if test="is(pm[3]=1 or pm[3]=4)"]]an overestimate[[elif test="is(pm[3]=5)"]]the exact area[[else]]an underestimate[[/if]].

  4. \(y = {@fr[4]@}\), \({@lr[4]@} \le x \le {@hr[4]@}\): \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = {@diff(fr[4],x,2)@}\), [[if test="is(pm[4]<=2)"]]never negative on this interval, so the curve bends upwards[[elif test="is(pm[4]<=4)"]]never positive on this interval, so the curve bends downwards[[else]]so the graph is a straight line[[/if]]. The {@rr[4]@} rule gives [[if test="is(pm[4]=1 or pm[4]=4)"]]an overestimate[[elif test="is(pm[4]=5)"]]the exact area[[else]]an underestimate[[/if]].

  5. \(y = {@fr[5]@}\), \({@lr[5]@} \le x \le {@hr[5]@}\): \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = {@diff(fr[5],x,2)@}\), [[if test="is(pm[5]<=2)"]]never negative on this interval, so the curve bends upwards[[elif test="is(pm[5]<=4)"]]never positive on this interval, so the curve bends downwards[[else]]so the graph is a straight line[[/if]]. The {@rr[5]@} rule gives [[if test="is(pm[5]=1 or pm[5]=4)"]]an overestimate[[elif test="is(pm[5]=5)"]]the exact area[[else]]an underestimate[[/if]].

questiondescription.text:
Integration: over- and underestimates from the bend of the curve

Grade 12 CBE Core 4.2: Decide whether trapezoidal and mid-ordinate estimates are over- or underestimates from the bend of the curve.

Core

This question is original to this project.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text: You reversed both trapezoidal rows. Sketch \(y = {@fr[rw[1]]@}\), which bends upwards, and join two points on it with a chord: is the chord above or below the curve? Do the same for \(y = {@fr[rw[3]]@}\), which bends downwards.

You reversed both mid-ordinate rows. The mid-ordinate rule errs the opposite way to the trapezoidal rule. Decide what the trapezoidal rule would do for \(y = {@fr[rw[2]]@}\), which bends upwards, and for \(y = {@fr[rw[4]]@}\), which bends downwards, then reverse it.
\(y = {@fr[rw[5]]@}\) is a straight line: it bends neither way. Sketch one strip under a straight line: how much area does the {@rr[rw[5]]@} rule gain or lose?

falsefeedback.text: \({@ncorrect@}\) of \(5\) are right. Decide the bend first (\(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) positive: bends upwards), then the rule: trapezia overestimate when the curve bends upwards, and the mid-ordinate rule errs the other way.
